title: The Role of Dwell Time on Advancing 3D Nano-printing of Complex Iron Nanostructure Geometries using Focused Electron Beam Induced Deposition
content: The shift from two- to three-dimensional structures is not only a prominent trend in nanomagnetism but also reflects a broader movement across nanotechnology as a whole [1,2]. Fields such as nanoelectronics [3], nanophotonics [4], data storage are poised to benefit from a new generation of greener, more versatile and multifunctional technologies enabled by this transition to 3D structures. While significant challenges remain, recent progress in bottom-up lithography, advanced microscopy, and computational techniques has made the future realization of these advancements increasingly feasible. Focused electron beam-induced deposition (FEBID), as shown in figure 1, is a cutting-edge direct-write nanofabrication technique used to manipulate matter at the nanoscale [5–8], combined with the unique magnetic properties of nanomaterials. It has gained significant attention in recent decades due to its potential applications in magnetic memories, such as racetrack memory. Consequently, substantial efforts have been directed toward developing nanofabrication techniques and characterizing magnetic nanoelements of various metal depositions. The high vapor pressure of precursors for materials such as Pt [1] and Co [9] is particularly advantageous for 3D nanoprinting under electron-limited conditions [7,10], where a high precursor flux is beneficial. Consequently, 3D-FEBID performs best with precursors that exhibit high vapor pressure [1]. In contrast, Fe deposition presents challenges due to its precursors having relatively lower vapor pressure. One reported solution was increasing the pressure; however, it has the opposite effect, hindering 3D nanoprinting [11].
